Izzo - CMS-0062-P Public Comment - Page 1 
Public Comment on CMS-0062-P 
Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs 
Re: CMS-0062-P; 91 FR 19890; RIN 0938-AV44 
Subject: Operational Performance, Interoperability Standards, Electronic Prior Authorization for Drugs, 
Adoption, Training, Sustainment, and Human Clinical Review 
Commenter: Christopher Izzo, Individual Commenter 
Position and Core Recommendation 
CMS's proposed HL7 FHIR-based prior authorization requirements and the National Council for 
Prescription Drug Programs (NCPDP) pharmacy standards present a meaningful opportunity to improve 
electronic prior authorization for drugs covered under medical and pharmacy benefits. A useful addition 
to the final rule would be an operational performance layer to help CMS assess whether interoperability 
conformance translates into usable workflows for prescribers, pharmacies, care teams, and patients after 
go-live. Key technical measures include API availability, usage reporting, denial-reason fields, Coverage 
Requirements Discovery (CRD), Documentation Templates and Rules (DTR), Prior Authorization Support 
(PAS), NCPDP SCRIPT, Formulary & Benefit, and Real-Time Prescription Benefit standards. Adoption 
and burden-reduction metrics would give CMS a clearer way to evaluate whether implementation 
reduces manual workarounds, improves medication-access coordination, and protects timely therapy in 
practice (Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services [CMS], 2026; U.S. Department of Health and Human 
Services [HHS], CMS, & Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology [ONC], 
2026). 
I support modernizing interoperability standards and prior authorization for drugs. The final rule would be 
stronger if CMS paired the proposed technical requirements with operational safeguards that address 
denial specificity, status visibility, specialty-level medication-access surveillance, workflow burden 
reduction, provider and pharmacy adoption, deployment funding clarity, sustainment governance, 
technical assistance, and human clinical review for high-risk medication decisions. 
Recommended Operational Safeguards 
1. Exact denial rationales: Denial responses should identify the missing documentation, coverage 
criterion, medical-necessity basis, step therapy requirement, formulary restriction, quantity limit, or 
clinical pathway requirement that drove the denial. 
2. Real-time authorization status visibility: Prescribers, pharmacies, patients, and care teams should 
have usable status visibility to reduce rework, duplicate submissions, and medication-access delays. 
3. Specialty-level medication access and outcome reporting: Reporting should detect access and 
outcome risk in high-burden areas such as oncology, behavioral health, specialty pharmacy, and 
chronic disease treatment. 
4. Interoperability and pharmacy workflow burden metrics: CMS should monitor FHIR/NCPDP-
enabled workflow performance, documentation effort, submission-to-decision time, duplicate 
requests, resubmissions, appeals, manual workarounds, claims disruption, medication abandonment, 
and provider/pharmacy workload. 
5. Provider and pharmacy adoption metrics: Metrics should distinguish true electronic prior 
authorization use from continued reliance on payer portals, fax, phone calls, manual workarounds, 
and duplicate documentation. 
6. Implementation accountability, funding clarity, training, and adoption requirements: CMS 
should clarify the responsibilities of impacted payer, vendor, pharmacy, and provider groups for 
upgrades, testing, training, dashboards, support, escalation, optimization, and sustainment. 
Izzo - CMS-0062-P Public Comment - Page 2 
7. Human clinical review for high-risk medication decisions: Human clinical review should occur 
before a denial involving high-risk medication access interrupts time-sensitive therapy, triggers 
treatment substitution, prevents dispensing, or overrides a treating clinicianâ€™s care plan. 
Operational Experience and Implementation Context 
My comments draw on more than two decades of leading enterprise health system operations and 
federal modernization efforts. Across those environments, interoperability standards, HIPAA-compliant 
information exchange, patient-centered safety, clinical workflow reliability, medication-access operations, 
pharmacy coordination, reimbursement integrity, user adoption, and sustainment governance had to work 
together at scale. That experience informs my concern that technical conformance alone will not protect 
patients or reduce burden unless CMS also measures operational readiness, adoption, accountability, 
and post-go-live performance. 
The CMS program-specific obligations fall primarily on impacted payers, while HHSâ€™s proposed HIPAA 
Administrative Simplification standards may also affect HIPAA-covered entities that electronically 
exchange covered prior authorization transactions. Prescribers, pharmacies, clinics, private practices, 
and health systems serving affected patients may still bear downstream implementation burdens if 
interoperable workflow redesign, training, upgrades, dashboards, and sustainment remain local 
responsibilities. CMS should clarify whether the final rule or accompanying guidance identifies any 
deployment funding, reimbursement pathway, incentive structure, Medicaid or Childrenâ€™s Health 
Insurance Program matching mechanism where applicable, vendor responsibility, or technical assistance 
for electronic health record upgrades, pharmacy system changes, interface testing, staff training, 
reporting dashboards, workflow redesign, and post-go-live optimization. Without that clarification, payer-
side compliance could unintentionally shift unfunded implementation costs to delivery systems and 
pharmacies. 
Why Technical Conformance Is Not Enough 
The key implementation risk is not whether interoperable electronic prior authorization for drugs can 
move information faster. The risk is whether impacted payers can return unresolved work to prescribers, 
pharmacies, care teams, and patients while still appearing compliant with technical requirements. A 
faster, vague, or repeatedly documented denial does not reduce burden. 
Salzbrenner et al. (2022) found that providers using electronic prior authorization reported faster approval 
times but did not report less time spent preparing or submitting requests. Salzbrenner et al. linked 
persistent burden to partial adoption, limited real-time exchange, weak clinical information exchange, and 
poor workflow integration. Salzbrenner et al. (2023) also found that step therapy, communication 
problems, and documentation requirements shaped prescribing behavior. These findings support a final 
rule that measures total operational burden, not transaction speed alone. 
Sahni et al. (2024) estimated that prior authorization accounts for approximately $35 billion in U.S. 
administrative spending and that provider time spent on prior authorization exceeds 100,000 full-time 
registered nurses annually. Faster electronic transactions may improve response times, but speed alone 
does not reduce the enterprise burden when coverage-requirement lookup, documentation preparation, 
pharmacy coordination, resubmission activity, appeal workload, claims adjudication disruption, 
dispensing delay, and manual workaround activity remain unresolved. 
Patient Access, Specialty-Level Monitoring, and Trust 
Patients face ethical, socioeconomic, and health outcome risks when prior authorization delays time-
sensitive therapy. Chino et al. (2023) found that 69% of oncology respondents experienced prior 
authorization-related delays, 73% of delayed respondents waited at least 2 weeks, and 22% did not 
receive recommended care due to delays or denials. Chino et al. also found that 89% trusted insurers 
less and 83% trusted the health care system less after prior authorization. 
Izzo - CMS-0062-P Public Comment - Page 3 
Specialty-level monitoring is necessary because aggregate payer metrics can obscure medication-
access harm across oncology, behavioral health, specialty pharmacy, and chronic disease treatment. 
Reporting should include access delays, denial rates, appeal outcomes, repeated documentation 
requests, resubmission frequency, treatment substitutions, medication abandonment, dispensing delays, 
and downstream effects on access to high-risk medications. Without specialty-level monitoring, a rule 
may appear successful at the aggregate level even as high-risk patient groups continue to experience 
delayed or disrupted therapy. 
HHS and CMS should also require governance safeguards for technology-supported or automated 
review processes, where used. Hou et al. (2026) identified algorithmic bias, privacy risks, workflow 
disruptions, and ambiguous accountability as concerns when health systems expand technology-
supported or automated review processes. Greene et al. (2025) found that only 20.2% of health care 
workers trusted leadership â€œvery much,â€ 42.9% reported low trust, and 97.7% reported professional 
effects of leadership trust. These findings support transparent accountability, human clinical escalation, 
implementation feedback loops, and sustainment metrics that protect workforce trust while preserving 
clinical judgment. 
Recommended Definition of Success 
Successful implementation should not be defined solely by API availability, endpoint reporting, 
interoperability conformance, or transaction volume. CMS should define success by accountable 
operational outcomes: high prescriber and pharmacy adoption, reduced portal and fax use, shorter 
authorization cycle times, fewer duplicate requests, fewer resubmissions and appeals, fewer dispensing 
delays, lower medication abandonment, clear escalation ownership, lower claims disruption, and 
specialty-level monitoring of high-risk medication access. 
CMS should consider finalizing CMS-0062-P to include explicit interoperability performance monitoring, 
specificity in denials, status visibility, specialty-level medication-access surveillance, workflow burden 
reduction, adoption reporting, implementation accountability, deployment funding clarity, sustainment 
governance, technical assistance for lower-resource settings, and human clinical review for high-risk 
medication decisions. These additions would preserve the ruleâ€™s interoperability goals while giving CMS a 
stronger way to evaluate whether electronic prior authorization for drugs improves real-world medication 
access rather than merely technical compliance. 
 
Izzo - CMS-0062-P Public Comment - Page 4

analysis:
## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Christopher Izzo, Individual Commenter
- **Stakeholder type:** Individual
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** More than two decades leading enterprise health system operations and federal modernization efforts involving interoperability, HIPAA-compliant exchange, medication-access operations, reimbursement integrity, user adoption, and sustainment governance.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The commenter supports modernizing electronic prior authorization for drugs through FHIR and NCPDP standards, but argues that technical conformance alone will not reduce burden or protect patients. He recommends adding an operational performance layer covering denial specificity, status visibility, specialty-level access monitoring, adoption metrics, implementation accountability, funding clarity, training, sustainment governance, technical assistance, and human clinical review for high-risk medication denials.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING; API-USAGE-METRICS; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS; GENERAL.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** 91 FR 19890; CMS-0062-P; RIN 0938-AV44. No specific CFR sections are cited.
- **Standards referenced:** HL7 FHIR; Da Vinci CRD, DTR, and PAS; NCPDP SCRIPT; NCPDP Formulary & Benefit; NCPDP Real-Time Prescription Benefit; HIPAA Administrative Simplification.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Operational performance monitoring**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** API availability and transaction volume do not show whether workflows reduce burden, duplicate requests, resubmissions, appeals, delays, or manual workarounds.
- **Specific request:** CMS should monitor workflow performance, documentation effort, submission-to-decision time, duplicate requests, resubmissions, appeals, claims disruption, medication abandonment, and provider/pharmacy workload.

**Topic 2: Specific denial rationales**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Support/Modify
- **Rationale:** Vague electronic denials can preserve or worsen burden even if transactions are faster.
- **Specific request:** Denials should identify the missing documentation, coverage criterion, medical-necessity basis, step therapy requirement, formulary restriction, quantity limit, or clinical pathway requirement.

**Topic 3: Real-time status visibility**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Prescribers, pharmacies, patients, and care teams need practical visibility to avoid duplicate work and medication-access delays.
- **Specific request:** Require usable status visibility across relevant participants.

**Topic 4: Specialty-level medication access monitoring**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Aggregate metrics can hide harm in oncology, behavioral health, specialty pharmacy, and chronic disease treatment.
- **Specific request:** Track access delays, denial rates, appeals, repeated documentation requests, resubmissions, treatment substitutions, medication abandonment, dispensing delays, and downstream effects by specialty or high-risk medication area.

**Topic 5: Implementation accountability and funding clarity**
- **Provision ID:** HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS; GENERAL
- **Position:** Clarify
- **Rationale:** Payer compliance may shift unfunded upgrade, testing, training, dashboard, and sustainment work to providers, pharmacies, and health systems.
- **Specific request:** Clarify responsibilities, funding/reimbursement pathways, incentives, Medicaid/CHIP matching mechanisms, vendor duties, and technical assistance.

**Topic 6: Human clinical review**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Automated or technology-supported review raises accountability, bias, trust, and patient safety concerns for high-risk medication decisions.
- **Specific request:** Require human clinical review before denials that interrupt time-sensitive therapy, trigger substitution, prevent dispensing, or override the treating clinician's plan.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S16:** The commenter responds directly by urging exact denial rationales that specify missing documentation, coverage criteria, medical-necessity bases, step therapy, formulary restrictions, quantity limits, or clinical pathway requirements.
- **S17:** The comment implies support for structured denial information by requesting specific denial fields and usable denial rationale content.
- **S29:** The commenter recommends metrics beyond API calls, including burden, workflow, resubmissions, appeals, claims disruption, dispensing delays, medication abandonment, and provider/pharmacy workload.
- **S30:** The commenter addresses governance of technology-supported review and privacy risks, but does not propose detailed privacy protections for metrics.
- **S34:** The comment supports ongoing post-go-live performance monitoring, though it does not specify a reporting frequency.
- **S35:** The commenter supports specialty-level and operational outcome reporting; publication details are not addressed.
- **S44-S51:** The comment recognizes that proposed HIPAA Administrative Simplification standards could affect all HIPAA-covered entities and highlights downstream implementation burden, workflow redesign, training, upgrades, and sustainment challenges.
- **S54-S55:** The commenter supports testing, governance, escalation, dashboards, and accountability mechanisms, including human clinical review for high-risk denials.
- **S66-S82:** The comment raises broader RFIs related to resiliency, adoption, workflow burden, specialty monitoring, and clinical oversight.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Add operational performance measures to determine whether interoperability reduces real-world burden.
2. Require exact, actionable denial rationales.
3. Provide real-time authorization status visibility to prescribers, pharmacies, patients, and care teams.
4. Monitor specialty-level medication access and outcomes in high-risk areas.
5. Track provider and pharmacy adoption separately from continued use of portals, fax, phone, and manual workarounds.
6. Clarify implementation responsibilities, funding, training, technical assistance, and sustainment governance.
7. Require human clinical review before high-risk medication denials disrupt time-sensitive therapy or override the treating clinician's plan.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Technical compliance without operational improvement; vague denials; lack of status visibility; hidden specialty-level access harms; unfunded downstream burden; inadequate governance of automated review.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Medication delays, treatment substitution, medication abandonment, claims disruption, reduced trust, provider and pharmacy workload, and shifted costs to delivery systems.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Partial adoption, limited real-time exchange, poor workflow integration, EHR and pharmacy system upgrades, interface testing, staff training, dashboards, escalation, and sustainment.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** Prior authorization estimated at approximately $35 billion in administrative spending; provider time exceeds 100,000 full-time registered nurses annually; oncology survey results including 69% delay experience, 73% waiting at least two weeks, and 22% not receiving recommended care due to delays or denials.
- **Studies or research referenced:** Salzbrenner et al. 2022 and 2023; Sahni et al. 2024; Chino et al. 2023; Hou et al. 2026; Greene et al. 2025.
- **Examples provided:** Oncology, behavioral health, specialty pharmacy, chronic disease treatment, payer portals, fax, phone calls, duplicate documentation, resubmissions, appeals, and claims disruption.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Patients, prescribers, pharmacies, care teams, health systems, impacted payers, vendors, Medicaid/CHIP agencies, and HIPAA-covered entities.
- **Economic implications:** Potential administrative savings if burden falls, but risk of unfunded implementation costs for providers and pharmacies.
- **Technical feasibility:** The commenter sees FHIR/NCPDP modernization as feasible but incomplete without adoption, workflow, testing, and sustainment measures.
- **Patient care impact:** Improved electronic PA could support timely therapy, but without safeguards high-risk patients may still experience delays, substitutions, abandonment, and loss of trust.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive with substantial modifications
- **Tone:** Professional, evidence-based, collaborative
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "Technical conformance alone will not protect patients or reduce burden unless CMS also measures operational readiness, adoption, accountability, and post-go-live performance." - Context: Explaining implementation risk.
2. "A faster, vague, or repeatedly documented denial does not reduce burden." - Context: Warning that electronic transactions may not equal operational improvement.
3. "Successful implementation should not be defined solely by API availability, endpoint reporting, interoperability conformance, or transaction volume." - Context: Recommending outcome-based success measures.
4. "Human clinical review should occur before a denial involving high-risk medication access interrupts time-sensitive therapy." - Context: Requesting clinical safeguards.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - The comment emphasizes post-go-live monitoring and sustainment, though it does not request a new compliance date.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - It raises unfunded implementation costs for providers, pharmacies, and health systems.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Reducing manual workarounds, duplicate documentation, appeals, and workload is central to the comment.
- [x] **PRIVACY-SECURITY** - It references privacy risks in automated or technology-supported review.
- [x] **HEALTH-EQUITY** - Specialty-level monitoring is framed as necessary to detect access risks in high-burden patient populations.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - The comment distinguishes standards conformance from operational readiness and workflow performance.
- [x] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - It relies on FHIR and NCPDP standards but seeks safeguards around implementation and usability.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Medication delays, abandonment, and high-risk therapy disruption are major concerns.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - It calls for clarified responsibilities among payers, vendors, pharmacies, providers, and agencies.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - It requests exact denial rationales, status visibility, and specialty-level reporting.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - The comment focuses on portals, fax, phone, duplicate documentation, and workflow integration.
- [x] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - EHR, pharmacy system, interface, and vendor responsibilities are explicitly raised.
